title: Techniques
description: Cross-genre skills: drum machines, mixing, modulation, randomness and ear training.
author: Strudel Workshop

skills.definition: Hear a drum pattern and write it down.

skills.name: Ear: pitch

tracks.title: Drum machines
tracks.blurb: One machine per lesson: the sound, the era, the pattern it is known for.

lessons.title: The TR-808
lessons.goal: Hear the 808: long boomy kick, snappy snare, the cowbell.
lessons.concept:
Roland’s TR-808 (1980) flopped as a drum machine and then defined electro, hip hop and Miami bass. Its kick is a long, tuned boom, its snare a snap of noise, and its **cowbell** is the most famous cowbell in music.

Same pattern, different machine: only `.bank()` changes.

tasks.text: Put the kick and the clap on the TR-808.
Add the 808 cowbell on beats 2 and 4, quiet.
tasks.hint: const bell = s("~ cb ~ cb").bank("RolandTR808").gain(.5), and stack it.

challenge.text: An 808 tom fill in the fourth bar only.
challenge.hint: const toms = s("<~ ~ ~ [lt mt ht ht]>").bank("RolandTR808").gain(.7), and stack it.

summary: The 808: long tuned kick, noise snare, the cowbell.
Only .bank() changes; the names stay.

lessons.title: The TR-909
lessons.goal: Hear the 909: punchy kick, sampled hats, the house machine.
lessons.concept: The TR-909 (1983) mixed analogue drums with **sampled** cymbals and hats. Its kick punches rather than booms, and its open hat “tss” on the offbeat is house music’s signature.

tasks.text: Move the kick and clap to the TR-909.
Add the 909 open hat on every offbeat.
tasks.hint: const hats = s("[~ oh]*4").bank("RolandTR909").gain(.5), and stack it.

challenge.text: Add the 909 ride on 8ths, quiet.
challenge.hint: const ride = s("rd*8").bank("RolandTR909").gain(.3), and stack it.

summary: The 909: punchy kick, sampled hats and cymbals.
Offbeat open hat = house.

lessons.title: The TR-707
lessons.goal: Hear the 707: the light, plastic Chicago machine.
lessons.concept: The TR-707 (1985) is all samples, thin and bright. It was cheap, so it was everywhere in early Chicago house: the “jack” rhythms were programmed on it, often with its **tambourine** running on 16ths.

tasks.text: Put the kick and clap on the TR-707.
Add the 707 tambourine on 16ths, quiet.
tasks.hint: const tamb = s("tb*16").bank("RolandTR707").gain(.3), and stack it.

challenge.text: Add the 707 cowbell on the “and” of 2 and 4.
challenge.hint: const bell = s("~ [~ cb] ~ [~ cb]").bank("RolandTR707").gain(.5), and stack it.

summary: The 707: thin, bright samples; the Chicago jack machine.
Tambourine on 16ths is its tell.

lessons.title: The TR-606
lessons.goal: Hear the 606: the tiny machine that came with the 303.
lessons.concept: The TR-606 (1981) was sold alongside the TB-303 as a “band in a box”. It has no clap: a sharp little snare, ticking hats and two toms. Its hats are the sound of early acid and of a lot of minimal techno.

tasks.text: Move the hats to the TR-606.
Add the 606 snare on 2 and 4 (it has no clap).
tasks.hint: const snare = s("~ sd ~ sd").bank("RolandTR606"), and stack it.

challenge.text: A 606 tom on the last 8th of the bar.
challenge.hint: const tom = s("~ ~ ~ [~ lt]").bank("RolandTR606").gain(.6), and stack it.

summary: The 606: ticking hats, a small snare, no clap.
The 303’s companion.

lessons.title: The LinnDrum
lessons.goal: Hear the LinnDrum: the sampled kit of 80s pop and boogie.
lessons.concept: The LinnDrum (1982) played real drum **samples** when everything else was analogue. Prince, Madonna and a thousand boogie records: a fat kick, a cracking snare, and a **shaker** that ran all through the song.

tasks.text: Put the kick on the LinnDrum, and swap the clap for its snare.
tasks.hint: .bank("LinnDrum") on the kick; const snare = s("~ sd ~ sd").bank("LinnDrum") instead of the clap.

tasks.text: Add the Linn shaker on 16ths.
tasks.hint: const shaker = s("sh*16").bank("LinnDrum").gain(.35), and stack it.

challenge.text: Add a Linn ride on 8ths.
challenge.hint: const ride = s("rd*8").bank("LinnDrum").gain(.3), and stack it.

summary: The LinnDrum: sampled drums, the 80s pop kit.
A shaker on 16ths is its groove.

lessons.title: The HR-16
lessons.goal: Hear the Alesis HR-16: cheap, clean, early house.
lessons.concept: The Alesis HR-16 (1987) was a cheap sampled kit with clean, slightly dull sounds. It turned up on lots of early house and techno records simply because producers could afford it.

tasks.text: Put the kick and clap on the HR-16.
Add its closed hats on 8ths.
tasks.hint: const hats = s("hh*8").bank("AlesisHR16").gain(.4), and stack it.

challenge.text: Add an HR-16 percussion hit on the “and” of 4.
challenge.hint: const perc = s("~ ~ ~ [~ perc]").bank("AlesisHR16").gain(.5), and stack it.

summary: The HR-16: cheap, clean samples on early house records.

lessons.title: The default kit
lessons.goal: Use the mixed kit that plays when there is no .bank().
lessons.concept: Leave `.bank()` off and Strudel plays its default kit: a mix of drums from many machines, with several **variations** of each sound. `bd:3` or `.n(3)` picks the fourth kick.

tasks.text: Remove .bank() from both parts to hear the default kit.
Pick the fourth kick variation.

challenge.text: Add the default kit’s ride on 8ths.
challenge.hint: const ride = s("rd*8").gain(.3), and stack it.

summary: No .bank(): the default mixed kit.
:n or .n(n) picks a variation.

lessons.title: Gain staging
lessons.goal: Set levels so nothing clips and the kick stays on top.
lessons.concept: Every part has a `.gain`. Push them past 1 and the output **clips**: a harsh crackle that gets worse as parts add up. The rule of thumb: nothing above 1, most parts well under it, and the **kick louder than anything else** so the groove reads on a club system.

tasks.text: Bring every part to 1 or below.
Put the kick on top: no part louder than it.

challenge.text: Add a clap at .5: quieter than the kick, present.
challenge.hint: const clap = s("~ cp ~ cp").bank("RolandTR909").gain(.5), and stack it.

summary: Nothing above 1; most parts well under.
The kick is the loudest thing.

lessons.title: Carving with high-pass
lessons.goal: Give each part its own frequency space.
lessons.concept:
Kick and bass own the lows. Everything else has lows it doesn’t need, and they pile up into **mud**. A **high-pass filter** on claps, hats and pads removes what isn’t helping, and the kick comes through.

There is no EQ in Strudel (gap G6); `.hpf` and `.lpf` are the tools.

tasks.text: High-pass the clap and the hats at 200 Hz or more.
tasks.hint: .hpf(300) on the clap and the hats.

tasks.text: High-pass the pad at 150 Hz or more, and leave the bass alone.

challenge.text: Keep the pad out of the hats’ way too: low-pass it below 5000 Hz.

summary: Kick and bass own the lows; high-pass everything else.
No EQ here: .hpf and .lpf do the carving.

lessons.title: One orbit per effect
lessons.goal: Stop two parts fighting over the same reverb and delay.
lessons.concept: Strudel has **one reverb and one delay per orbit**. Two parts on the same orbit with different settings overwrite each other, and the result is a silent, confusing mess (gap G4). Give each part that wants its own reverb or delay its own `.orbit(n)`.

tasks.text: Move the stab to orbit 2, so its small room and its delay are its own.
Add hats with their own little room on orbit 3.
tasks.hint: const hats = s("[~ oh]*4").bank("RolandTR909").gain(.4).room(.3).orbit(3), and stack it.

challenge.text: Keep the kick dry: make sure it stays on orbit 1 with no room.
challenge.hint: Nothing to add: check the kick line has no .room or .orbit, then add .room(0) to make it explicit.

summary: One reverb and one delay per orbit.
Each part with its own settings gets its own orbit.

lessons.title: Compression, per voice
lessons.goal: Even out a clap and a bass with a compressor.
lessons.concept:
A **compressor** turns the loud moments down so the quiet ones can come up: punch and glue. Strudel’s is per voice, written as one string: `"threshold:ratio:knee:attack:release"`. `-20:4:3:.01:.1` means start squashing above −20 dB, 4 to 1, gently, fast in, quick out.

There is no master-bus compressor (gap G6): each part gets its own.

tasks.text: Compress the clap.
Compress the bass, a little harder.

challenge.text: Make up the level the compressor took: .postgain(1.2) on the clap.
challenge.hint: .postgain(1.2) after the compressor on the clap line.

summary: .compressor("thr:ratio:knee:att:rel") evens a part out.
Per voice only: no master compressor here.

lessons.title: Ducking
lessons.goal: Make the bass dip whenever the kick hits.
lessons.concept:
**Sidechain ducking**: every kick hit pushes the bass down for a moment, so the two never fight and the track pumps. The kick does the ducking: `.duckorbit(2)` names the orbit to duck, `.duckdepth` how far, `.duckattack` how fast it comes back.

The ducked orbit must have something playing on it, or Strudel throws an error (gap G14).

tasks.text: Duck the bass’s orbit from the kick, fairly deep.
Let it come back a little slower.

challenge.text: Pump harder: depth .9.

summary: The kick ducks an orbit: .duckorbit, .duckdepth, .duckattack.
The ducked orbit must be playing.

lessons.title: What needs a DAW
lessons.goal: Mix with the tools Strudel has, and know which ones it lacks.
lessons.concept: Strudel has **no EQ** (no shelves, no parametric bands) and **no master limiter or bus compressor** (gap G6). What it has: `.gain` for level, `.hpf` and `.lpf` to carve, per-voice `.compressor`, and ducking. That gets a loop clean and punchy. A finished release still goes through a DAW for EQ, bus compression and limiting, and there is no shame in that.

tasks.text: Carve: high-pass the clap, hats and pad at 150 Hz or more.
tasks.hint: .hpf(200) on the clap, the hats and the pad.

tasks.text: Level: bring the clap and hats to .6 and the bass to .7, below the kick.
tasks.hint: .gain(.6) on the clap and hats, .gain(.7) on the bass.

challenge.text: Tame the pad’s top with a low-pass at 4000 Hz, the nearest thing to a high shelf.

summary: No EQ, no master limiter: carve with hpf/lpf, level with gain.
A release still goes through a DAW.

lessons.title: Signal shapes
lessons.goal: Move a cutoff with sine, saw and square waves.
lessons.concept: A **signal** is a value that changes over time. `sine` rises and falls smoothly; `saw` ramps up and drops; `square` jumps between low and high. `.range(a, b)` scales it; `.slow(n)` stretches one cycle over n bars.

tasks.text: Make the cutoff a sine between 300 and 1500 Hz over 4 bars.
Now a saw: a ramp up over 4 bars, then back to the bottom.

challenge.text: A square: two bars open, two bars closed.

summary: sine, saw, square: smooth, ramp, jump.
.range scales; .slow stretches.

lessons.title: Perlin and rand
lessons.goal: Random values, smooth or jumpy, on a control.
lessons.concept: `rand` is a new random value for every event: jittery, lively. `perlin` is random but smooth: it drifts. Use `rand` on hat levels for a human feel, `perlin` on a filter for slow weather.

tasks.text: Give the hats a random gain between .2 and .6.
Let perlin wander the pad’s cutoff between 400 and 2000 Hz over 8 bars.

challenge.text: Scatter the hats across the stereo field with rand on pan.

summary: rand jumps per event; perlin drifts.

lessons.title: Stepped sweeps
lessons.goal: Make a sweep move on a held note with .segment.
lessons.concept: A signal is read **once per event** (gap G3). A pad that holds one chord per bar reads its cutoff once per bar, so a sweep comes out as steps. `.segment(16)` chops the pad into 16 events per bar, so the sweep moves 16 times a bar.

tasks.text: Chop the pad into 16 events per bar so the sweep moves inside the bar.

challenge.text: Coarser steps: 4 per bar.

summary: Signals are read once per event.
.segment(n) retriggers n times a bar so a sweep moves on held notes.

lessons.title: Tremolo and auto-pan
lessons.goal: Put a signal on gain and on pan.
lessons.concept: A signal on **gain** is a tremolo: the level pulses. A signal on **pan** is an auto-pan: the sound swings between the speakers. Both need the part chopped with `.segment` so the signal is read often enough.

tasks.text: Tremolo: a sine between .2 and .5 on the pad’s gain, four times a bar.
Auto-pan: a sine across the stereo field over 2 bars.

challenge.text: A triangle wave on the pan instead of a sine.

summary: Signal on gain: tremolo. Signal on pan: auto-pan.
Chop the part with .segment first.

lessons.title: The 16-bar sweep
lessons.goal: Automate a filter and its resonance over a whole phrase.
lessons.concept: The classic tension tool: a cutoff that opens over 16 bars while the resonance moves on its own clock. Long `.slow` values turn a signal into **automation**.

tasks.text: Open the acid cutoff from 300 to 3000 Hz over 16 bars.
Move the resonance between 10 and 22 on an 8-bar sine.

challenge.text: Add hats whose high-pass rises over the same 16 bars.

summary: Long .slow values are automation.
Move cutoff and resonance on different clocks.

lessons.title: Drop some hits
lessons.goal: Thin a pattern out at random with degradeBy.
lessons.concept: `.degradeBy(p)` drops each event with probability p. Strudel’s randomness is **deterministic**: the same code gives the same result every time, so a loop can be random and still repeatable.

tasks.text: Drop about a third of the hats.
Do the same with mini-notation: a ? after the step.

challenge.text: Add rimshots on 8ths that only play half the time.

summary: .degradeBy(p) and ? drop events at random.
Strudel’s randomness repeats exactly.

lessons.title: Sometimes
lessons.goal: Change a random share of events with sometimesBy.
lessons.concept: `.sometimesBy(p, f)` applies a function to a share of the events: pitch some rimshots up, make some hats quieter. `.sometimes`, `.often` and `.rarely` are shortcuts for 50%, 75% and 25%.

tasks.text: Pitch about a third of the rimshots up an octave.
Make a fifth of the hats very quiet.

challenge.text: Rarely double a rimshot.

summary: .sometimesBy(p, f) changes a share of events.
sometimes / often / rarely are shortcuts.

lessons.title: Choose
lessons.goal: Pick a random value from a list on every event.
lessons.concept: `choose(a, b, c)` returns one of its values at random for each event. On gain it makes accents; on scale degrees it writes a random melody that stays in key.

tasks.text: Hats at either .2 or .6, chosen per hit.
A random bass line from degrees 0, 3 and 5.
tasks.hint: n(choose(0, 3, 5)).struct("x*8") instead of n("0*8") on the bass.

challenge.text: Pan each hat hard left or hard right.

summary: choose(…) picks a value per event.
On degrees it writes a melody that stays in key.

lessons.title: Seeds
lessons.goal: Pick a different, repeatable random variation.
lessons.concept: Because Strudel’s randomness is deterministic, you can **choose which version** you get: `.seed(n)` gives a different but equally repeatable set of random choices. Try seeds until the pattern feels right, and it stays that way.

tasks.text: Set a seed on the hats.
Try another: seed 7.

challenge.text: Add a rimshot pattern with its own seed, so it varies apart from the hats.

summary: .seed(n) picks a repeatable random variation.

lessons.title: Ear: a kick pattern
lessons.goal: Hear a kick pattern and write it.
lessons.concept: Press ▶ Play the reference and count along: 1 2 3 4. Where do the kicks land?

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.
tasks.hint: s("bd ~ bd bd"): kicks on 1, 3 and 4.

summary: Listen first, then write.

lessons.title: Ear: a clap pattern
lessons.goal: Hear a clap pattern with a double and write it.
lessons.concept: Claps on 2 and 4 are the usual; listen for the extra one.

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.
tasks.hint: s("~ cp ~ [cp cp]"): the fourth beat is two claps.

summary: Listen first, then write.

lessons.title: Ear: closed and open hats
lessons.goal: Hear where the open hats fall among the closed ones.
lessons.concept: Eight hat hits per bar; two of them are open. Which two?

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.
tasks.hint: s("[hh hh oh hh]*2"): the open hat is the third 8th of each half.

summary: Listen first, then write.

lessons.title: Ear: a two-bar kick phrase
lessons.goal: Hear a kick pattern that changes in the second bar.
lessons.concept: Count two bars. The first is plain; the second has a variation at the end.

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.

summary: Listen first, then write.

lessons.title: Ear: two notes
lessons.goal: Hear a two-note bass and write the notes.
lessons.concept: The first note is a C. Is the second higher or lower, and by how much? (It is a minor third up.)

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.

summary: Listen first, then write.

lessons.title: Ear: a three-note riff
lessons.goal: Hear a riff and write its notes.
lessons.concept: Three notes going up, then a rest. They are the first three notes of a minor chord.

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.

summary: Listen first, then write.

lessons.title: Ear: minor or major
lessons.goal: Hear two chords and tell which is minor and which is major.
lessons.concept: Bar 1 and bar 2 play a chord each on the same root. One is sad (minor, flat third), one bright (major). Write them in the order you hear.

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.

summary: Listen first, then write.

lessons.title: Ear: the roots of a progression
lessons.goal: Hear a four-chord progression and write its bass roots.
lessons.concept: Four bars, one chord each. Follow the lowest note: it starts on C and moves. Write the four root notes as a bassline.

tasks.text: Listen with ▶ Play the reference, then write what you hear.
tasks.hint: chord("<Cm7 Fm7 Ab^7 Gm7>").rootNotes(2): C, F, Ab, G.

summary: Listen first, then write.
